standard.title: Materials, systems, components, tools and equipment in designed solutions
standard.description: analyse and make judgements on how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined to create designed solutions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined to create designed solutions (AC9TDE8K06). They can identify material properties and justify selection decisions. They have not yet made judgements on combinations, nor critiqued environmental consequences of material selection, nor investigated emerging and innovative materials at this level.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse and make judgements on how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined in designed solutions — including environmental consequences of material selection, emerging materials, and justified selection from a broad technology range.

nodes.label: Environmental consequences of material selection
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can critique designed solutions to identify the environmental consequences of material selection and compare with sustainable alternatives.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one environmental consequence of a material used in an existing product; describe one alternative material that would reduce that consequence.
nodes.typical_width: Critique an existing product's material selection for environmental consequences — considering carbon footprint, toxicity, biodegradability, and end-of-life options; research at least one emerging or sustainable alternative and evaluate the trade-offs of switching.
wider: Critique the design of common plastic bags and research innovative sustainable alternatives (bioplastics, seaweed-based materials) — make a judgement on which alternative best balances performance, cost and environmental benefit

Analyse how First Nations Australians' use of possum fur (thermal properties, biodegradability, source management) represents sophisticated material knowledge — examine how this is being applied in contemporary high-performance thermal clothing

Investigate how locally sourced materials (e.g. bamboo cross-laminated timber) compare to conventional equivalents on carbon footprint, performance and cost — justify a selection decision for a specific application

response_modes.reason: Environmental consequences of material selection are highly context-dependent — plastics, textiles, structural materials and fibres each have different environmental profiles and different alternative options. Multiple material contexts build analytical flexibility rather than a single-material conclusion.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations material knowledge (possum fur thermal properties) and its contemporary commercial application is substantively rich — it connects historical material science to active product development and raises intellectual property questions worth investigating.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one environmental consequence of a specific material selection
Evaluates an alternative material against the original — not just describes it
nodes.hinge_reason: Critiquing environmental consequences of material selection at N1 directly informs N2 judgements about emerging materials — students who haven't developed this evaluative lens cannot make defensible sustainability judgements about new materials.

nodes.label: Emerging and innovative materials
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate emerging materials and make judgements on their impact on design decisions.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one emerging material and explain how it changes at least one design decision compared to a conventional material.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate multiple emerging materials (e.g. bioplastics from waste, soft robotics nanomaterials, fibre-based medical textiles) across different application domains; make judgements about how each changes design possibilities, constraints and sustainability trade-offs.
wider: Investigate bioplastic material made from discarded potato peels — evaluate its properties, applications (buttons, eyeglasses) and limitations compared to conventional plastics

Examine fibre-based medical textiles (e.g. collagen fibre sutures with silk-like strength and biodegradability) — analyse how the combination of properties creates a design solution conventional materials cannot achieve
Investigate soft robotics nanomaterials that enable robot components to function like human muscles — evaluate what design possibilities this opens and what engineering challenges remain

response_modes.reason: Emerging material judgements develop best across multiple material types — bioplastics, nanomaterials, medical textiles and renewable composites each illuminate different aspects of what makes a material viable for design. A single emerging material provides insufficient range for the 'make judgements' command term.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of emerging materials — waste-based bioplastics, medical textiles, soft robotics nanomaterials — is genuinely rich for advancing students. Each application domain reveals different material property trade-offs and different design implications.
success_criteria: Describes a specific emerging material's relevant properties
Makes a judgement about how it changes design decisions compared to a conventional alternative

nodes.label: Justifying selection from a broad technology range
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can justify the selection of specific materials, tools, equipment, processes and systems from a broad range of technology options for a design context.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a design context, select and justify at least two technology choices (e.g. material + tool, or process + component) with reference to the design requirements.
nodes.typical_width: Justify selection decisions across materials, tools, equipment, processes and components for a design project — referencing requirements such as sustainability, safety, accessibility, cost, weight and performance; explain why alternatives were not selected and what the implications of different choices would be.
wider: Justify the selection of low-emission paints and locally sourced materials (e.g. bamboo CLT) for a specific building application — evaluate the sustainability, structural and cost implications
Justify technology selection for minimising product weight to reduce transport costs in a rural Australian context — analyse what properties must be balanced and what the selection criteria are
Evaluate a design decision to use compressive vs tensile materials in a structural application — calculate or estimate the relevant forces and justify the selection

response_modes.reason: Justification requires students to reason from requirement to selection to trade-off — without this structure, students select by familiarity or preference rather than by analysed fit. The scaffold (what does this application require? → which options meet each requirement? → what are the trade-offs? → which combination best fits?) produces genuine justification.

success_criteria: Selection is justified with reference to specific design requirements — not just preferences
At least one trade-off is acknowledged — why the chosen option is better than at least one alternative for this context
nodes.hinge_reason: The descriptor's command term is 'analyse and make judgements' — students who cannot justify technology selection with structured reasoning against design requirements produce descriptions rather than judgements, failing the descriptor.
